column1: # VS Code extensions that shipped malware. One line each, tab separated. After editing, run: bash tools/gen.sh
#   id        publisher.name, as the extension's folder spells it (compared without case)
#   version   the exact version, or * when every version is malware
#   incident  an id from data/incidents.tsv, whose level must be act
#   registry  openvsx: the bad build was only ever published to Open VSX, so it is looked for in the
#             extension folders of the editors that install from there (Cursor, Windsurf and Devin
#             Desktop, VSCodium and Kiro) and not in VS Code's own, where the same id is the
#             Marketplace's extension: a clean build, or another publisher's. any: looked for in
# Looked for as <id>-<version> folders (a platform suffix such as -darwin-arm64 may follow).
# GlassWorm, from Socket's posts, each wave its own incident. A version where the post gives one, every
# version (*) where it names the extension without one: these are the attacker's own extensions, which
# update themselves, so a version from before an extension was turned counts too. Left out: what a post
# calls a sleeper (not malicious yet), and the 17 extensions turned on 29 April, whose payload Open VSX
# had already removed (the April post's update).
#   January 2026: the four oorzc versions, Open VSX only (Socket says the publisher's Marketplace listings
#     were not compromised, and the Marketplace has a clean oorzc.ssh-tools 0.5.1 of March 2026), and
#     the thirteen earlier extensions it lists, which were never on the Marketplace.
#   13 March 2026: the 72 extensions listed since that report, less those thirteen.
#   18 March 2026: the versions the post shows delivering malware, themselves or through an extension pack.
#   25 April 2026: the six it confirms as malicious; its 67 sleepers are left out.
#   2 October 2026: the two malicious Marketplace themes; Cosmic Nebula is on Open VSX too.
